As an economics student at Hogwarts, the Ministry of Magic has tasked you with analyzing the impact of policy proposals on three firms in the cauldron industry, given their distinct cost structures:

**The Cauldron Co.** is a large, established firm producing high-quality cauldrons with traditional methods. They have high fixed costs but low, constant marginal costs due to economies of scale.

**The Witching Hour** is a smaller firm specializing in novelty cauldrons. They have moderate fixed costs but increasing marginal costs due to specialized production.

**Nimbus Cauldron Works** is a new entrant producing low-cost, mass-produced cauldrons made to order by a contract foundry. They have no meaningful fixed costs, and low constant marginal costs.

## Q1 | {++The Witching Hour’s Workshop++}

{++The Witching Hour makes its novelty cauldrons by hand. The table shows how many cauldrons the workshop makes in a day with each number of workers. Each worker is paid 60 coins a day, and the workshop pays 120 coins a day in rent however many cauldrons it makes.++}

::: {.table style=grid inset=7pt columns="auto auto 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr" fills=r0:gray-dark valign=middle}

| {++**Workers**++} | {++**Cauldrons**++} | {++**Marginal product**++} | {++**Variable cost**++} | {++**Total cost**++} | {++**ATC**++} |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| {++0++} | {++0++} | — | [0]{.red} | [120]{.red} | — |
| {++1++} | {++15++} | [15]{.red} | [60]{.red} | [180]{.red} | [12]{.red} |
| {++2++} | {++24++} | [9]{.red} | [120]{.red} | [240]{.red} | [10]{.red} |
| {++3++} | {++30++} | [6]{.red} | [180]{.red} | [300]{.red} | [10]{.red} |
| {++4++} | {++32++} | [2]{.red} | [240]{.red} | [360]{.red} | [11.25]{.red} |

:::

a\) {++Fill in the marginal product of each worker. What happens to the marginal product as workers are added?++}

::: solution

The marginal products are 15, 9, 6 and 2. Each added worker adds fewer cauldrons than the one before: the marginal product is diminishing.

:::

b\) {++Fill in the variable cost, total cost, and average total cost at each number of workers.++}

::: solution

Variable cost is the wage bill, $60 \times L$. Total cost adds the rent of 120. Average total cost is total cost divided by cauldrons: $180/15 = 12$, $240/24 = 10$, $300/30 = 10$, $360/32 = 11.25$. It falls, flattens, then rises.

:::

c\) {++The first worker costs 60 coins and adds 15 cauldrons. The fourth worker costs 60 coins and adds 2 cauldrons. What does each cauldron add to total cost in each case? Use your answer to explain why The Witching Hour has increasing marginal costs.++}

::: solution

The first worker’s cauldrons each add $60/15 = 4$ coins to total cost. The fourth worker’s cauldrons each add $60/2 = 30$ coins. Every worker costs the same, but later workers add fewer cauldrons, so each extra cauldron costs more. Diminishing marginal product is the reason marginal cost rises. (The third worker’s cauldrons each add $60/6 = 10$, the same as average total cost at 30 cauldrons: marginal cost meets $ATC$ at its lowest point.)

:::

## Q2 | Cost Curves {++and Policies++}

Graph all three firms’ average total cost and marginal cost curves. {++Then show how each firm’s curves shift with its policy: a lump sum tax on The Cauldron Co., a per unit (*called specific*) tax on The Witching Hour, and a per unit (*called specific*) subsidy on Nimbus Cauldron Works.++}

<!-- Editor. The question gives no numbers, so the curves are illustrative: The Cauldron Co. FC 600, MC 10; The Witching Hour FC 200, MC = 6 + q/2 (ATC lowest at q = 28.3, where ATC = MC = 20.1); Nimbus MC = ATC = 12. They agree with the ink key ../../E_Practice_Bank/Vignette_E1_cauldron-costs_sols_F24.pdf (checked 2026-11-12). -->

::: solution

*The original curves (dashed in the graphs).*

**The Cauldron Co.** Marginal cost is constant, so $MC$ is a flat line. The high fixed cost is spread over more cauldrons as output grows, so $ATC = MC + FC/q$ starts high and falls toward $MC$ without ever reaching it.

**The Witching Hour.** Marginal cost rises with output, so $MC$ slopes up. At low output the fixed cost dominates and $ATC$ falls; once $MC$ rises above $ATC$ it pulls the average up. $ATC$ is U-shaped and $MC$ crosses it at its lowest point.

**Nimbus Cauldron Works.** With no fixed cost and a constant marginal cost, every cauldron costs the same to make, so the average equals the marginal: $ATC = MC$, one flat line.

*The shifts (solid).*

**The Cauldron Co.** A lump sum tax is the same amount however much the firm makes, so it acts like a fixed cost. Marginal cost does not move. Average total cost rises by the tax divided by output, so it rises most at low output and the gap closes as output grows.

**The Witching Hour.** A per unit tax is paid on every cauldron, so every cauldron costs that much more to make. Marginal cost and average total cost both shift up by the tax at every output, and the lowest point of $ATC$ stays at the same output.

**Nimbus Cauldron Works.** A per unit subsidy pays the firm on every cauldron, so every cauldron costs that much less to make. Its single flat line, $MC = ATC$, shifts down by the subsidy.

(Drawn with a lump sum tax of 300 coins and a per unit tax and subsidy of 4 coins.)

:::
